claims.text: The target material is a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy.
Introducing grain-boundary segregation can improve resistance to thermally induced toughness loss in high-entropy alloys.
Boron or carbon could serve as the segregating element responsible for the proposed improvement.
The hypothesis should hold after exposure at approximately 600°C for approximately 100 hours.
Reduced grain-boundary energy and improved cohesion reduce the tendency for grain-boundary embrittlement.
Reduced grain-boundary embrittlement improves resistance to thermally induced toughness loss.
The segregated alloy will retain at least 20% more toughness than an otherwise comparable alloy without grain-boundary segregation.
The proposed toughness improvement will be most significant above 500°C.
The proposed toughness improvement will be most significant after exposure longer than 50 hours.
The exact amount and identity of the required segregant are uncertain.
Charpy impact testing will be used to measure toughness.
Atom-probe tomography will be used to measure grain-boundary segregation.
The hypothesis is falsified if the segregated alloy shows less than a 10% toughness increase relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes introduction of a specific amount and the intervention implies a specific segregating element, but neither is specified and the uncertainty field states that the exact amount and element remain unknown.

The predicted outcome requires at least a 20% toughness increase, whereas falsification is defined only below 10%; outcomes from 10% to under 20% would fail the prediction without falsifying the hypothesis.
